Quotations originally in French, retranslated from the French: Rousseau (Confessions, Book VI, the princess and the brioche), Alphonse Karr (Les Guêpes, 1841 and 1843), Madame de Boigne (Mémoires, remark attributed to Madame Victoire).

titre: Marie-Antoinette's Brioche, a Line Older Than She Is
accroche: Rousseau tells the brioche anecdote in his Confessions, five years before Marie-Antoinette arrived in France.
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 1765, in Môtiers, Jean-Jacques Rousseau writes the sixth book of his *Les Confessions* (The Confessions). There he tells a very personal memory: a penniless young servant, he sometimes dreamed of a good wine he could not afford, and consoled himself by recalling “the stopgap of a great princess who was told that the peasants had no bread, and who replied: Let them eat brioche.” Failing anything better, he writes, “I bought brioche.” The anecdote is no firebrand: it is an image of making do, not an attack on a queen; Rousseau names no one, and the book will not appear until 1782, four years after his death.

## A line written before its accused arrived

Here is the chronological problem. Marie-Antoinette, born in 1755 in Vienna, does not arrive in France until May 1770, to marry the future Louis XVI. Yet around 1765, Rousseau has already written this passage: the archduchess is then about ten years old and still living in Austria. She cannot possibly be the “great princess” whose remark Rousseau reports. The earliest association between this line and Marie-Antoinette appears nearly fifty years later, from the pen of the journalist Alphonse Karr, in his review *Les Guêpes* (The Wasps): in November 1841, he reports it cautiously, as a saying, “true or false,” attributed to the queen; in April 1843, far from asserting it, he calls it into question even more deeply, having found in a 1760 book (thus predating Marie-Antoinette's arrival in France) an almost identical sentence attributed to a Duchess of Tuscany, and concludes that “the saying was not said by Marie-Antoinette, but found again and put into circulation against her.”

## A line that has changed owners for three centuries

The most interesting thing is not that the line is false, it is that it keeps changing owners. The Duchess of Tuscany found by Karr is not the only other candidate: the memoirs of Madame de Boigne, for their part, report a similar version, about pâté crust rather than brioche, attributed to Madame Victoire, daughter of Louis XV: “But good heavens, if only they could resign themselves to eating pâté crust!” The motif (an aristocrat suggesting, with no apparent malice, a food she believes common to people who have no bread) thus circulates from one figure to another well before and well after Marie-Antoinette's reign, always attached to whoever, at the moment the story is told, best embodies an aristocracy cut off from the people.

Marie-Antoinette therefore did not invent the indifference of the powerful to missing bread: she inherited a line that had been looking for a mouth for decades, and her trial in collective memory offered it the most convenient and most lasting one, nearly half a century after her death in 1793.

carte.punch: Rousseau writes the brioche line five years before Marie-Antoinette arrives in France.
carte.idee: “Let them eat brioche” comes from Rousseau's Confessions, written around 1765-1769. Marie-Antoinette does not arrive in France until 1770. The association with the queen first appears, with doubt, in a journal in 1841, and its own author calls it into question two years later.

quiz.question: Why can the line “Let them eat brioche” not be Marie-Antoinette's?
choix: Because it is written in German in the original text
Because Rousseau wrote it before Marie-Antoinette arrived in France
Because the line comes from a speech given in the Assembly
quiz.explication: Rousseau writes the first six books of the Confessions between 1765 and 1769, when Marie-Antoinette, born in 1755, is still living in Austria: she does not arrive in France until 1770. Nothing points to a German version, an aversion to brioche, or a parliamentary origin: the association with the queen appears in a press article from 1841, with doubt, and its author will himself call it into question in 1843.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Madame de Boigne's memoirs, what similar version of the line circulates, and attributed to whom?
choix: About white bread, attributed to the Duchess of Tuscany
About table wine, attributed to Rousseau himself
About pâté crust, attributed to Madame Victoire, daughter of Louis XV
About pastries, attributed to Louis XV himself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Madame de Boigne's memoirs report the remark not about brioche but about pâté crust, attributing it to Madame Victoire, daughter of Louis XV, and not to Marie-Antoinette.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Alphonse Karr first associate the brioche line with Marie-Antoinette, and with what caution?
choix: In November 1841, in Les Guêpes, as a saying that may be true or false
In April 1843, in Les Guêpes, asserting it without reservation
In 1770, at Marie-Antoinette's arrival in France, as an established fact
In 1793, in a pamphlet published after the queen's death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Karr first reports the saying in November 1841 in Les Guêpes, presenting it with caution as a saying that may be true or false, not as an established fact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Rousseau say he did “failing anything better,” in the anecdote he reports in Book VI of the Confessions?
choix: He wrote a letter of protest to the king
He fasted for several days rather than complain
He begged for alms at a nearby convent
He recalled the great princess's remark and bought brioche
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rousseau writes that, unable to afford the wine he dreamed of, he recalled the great princess's remark about brioche and bought some.
